cues.text: Let us finish with a model essay answer.
The task is to optimise a slow patient-history query, and this answer shows how a strong response is structured.
Start with the definition.
Query optimisation is the process of choosing efficient physical operations while preserving a query's logical result.
Notice the two halves of that sentence.
The system is free to change how it does the work, but it must never change what the answer is.
The essay then describes the path a query takes.
The database management system, or DBMS, parses the SQL.
It validates its meaning.
It rewrites the logical plan.
It estimates the cost of alternative plans, and then it executes the plan it selected.
How does it estimate cost?
The cost model uses statistics, cardinality, I/O, CPU and memory.
In distributed systems it also uses communication.
Cardinality here means the number of rows an operation is expected to produce, and I/O means reading and writing data from storage.
Now the concrete case.
Imagine a query that selects a patient's latest 20 observations.
If the system uses a full scan, it may inspect many irrelevant records, and it may then have to sort a large result.
That is wasteful, because the patient we want is only a tiny part of the table.
The proposed fix is a composite B-tree index on patient identifier and timestamp.
Composite means the index is built on two columns together.
With patient identifier first, the index can locate the relevant key range for that one patient.
With timestamp second, it can return the recent records in order, so the large sort is avoided.
But the essay is careful to qualify this.
Whether the index is beneficial depends on selectivity, clustering, data size and write overhead.
Selectivity is how small a fraction of the table the query picks out.
Clustering concerns how the stored rows are physically arranged relative to the index.
Write overhead is the extra work every insert or update must do to maintain the index.
The source also states a limit: an index may not be useful when a query retrieves most of the table.
In that case, reading through the index would not beat simply scanning.
Next comes the method of proof, because an optimisation claim needs evidence.
The essay says: record the baseline with EXPLAIN and an appropriate execution-statistics tool.
Then add the index, and refresh statistics if needed, so the optimiser has current information.
Then repeat the trials on the same synthetic dataset, so that the comparison is fair and no real patient data is exposed.
What should be compared?
Scan types, actual versus estimated rows, examined records or pages, execution time and returned results.
And one rule is non-negotiable: the result must remain equivalent.
A faster query that returns a different answer is a failure.
The essay then mentions two further techniques.

A cache can help repeated safe reads, but it requires invalidation, meaning a way to remove or refresh stale entries, and it requires tenant-aware keys, so that one tenant's cached data is never served to another.
A materialised view can precompute historical aggregates, and it needs a refresh strategy based on acceptable staleness, that is, how out of date the stored results are allowed to be.
The essay's conclusion is that these techniques address distinct bottlenecks and must be chosen using measurements, not guesswork.
And finally, it widens the lens.
Query speed is not the only criterion.
A good solution must also maintain integrity, access controls, freshness and sustainable write performance.
In other words, the fastest query is not the best answer if it weakens correctness, security, currency of data, or the system's ability to keep accepting new writes.
